title: Reasoning about Reasoning: BAPO Bounds on Chain-of-Thought Token Complexity in LLMs
claim: Step-by-step generation can be modeled as a chain of bandwidth-limited prefix/suffix information exchanges, so each step needs only constant communication.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; token boxes with nested braces on left, split diagram on right
description: Two black-and-white panels. Panel (a) shows a row of boxes: a wide box for input x1…xn, then separate boxes for CoT tokens s1, s2, s3 … sm, then an output box y. Braces above label input, CoT reasoning and output. Below, nested braces of growing length are labeled BAPO step 1, BAPO step 2 and so on, showing that each generated token is its own BAPO step over a longer prefix. Panel (b) zooms into one step. A wide box holds x1…xk, a vertical line marking an arbitrary split (∀ splits k), then x_{k+1}…x_n s1…s_{t-1}. An arrow leads to the output token s_t. Two lines under the box carry the prefix summary f(·) of a bits and the attention g(·) of b tokens. Captions sit beneath each panel.
caption: Overview of our modeling approach. An LLM autoregressively generates reasoning tokens s1, · · · sm to eventually produce an answer y. Each token generation step is modeled using a bounded attention prefix oracle (BAPO) with constant bandwidths; see Section 2.2 for a formal definition. To produce each st, information in a BAPO can cross an arbitrary prefix/suffix cut only through an a-bit summary and up to b attended tokens from the prefix; this constrained update repeats for steps t = 1, . . . m + 1.
abstract: Inference-time scaling via chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is a major driver of state-of-the-art LLM performance, but it comes with substantial latency and compute costs. We address a fundamental theoretical question: how many reasoning tokens are required to solve a problem as input size grows? By extending the bounded attention prefix oracle (BAPO) model--an abstraction of LLMs that quantifies the information flow required to solve a task--we prove lower bounds on the CoT tokens required for three canonical BAPO-hard tasks: binary majority, triplet matching, and graph reachability. We show that each requires $Î©(n)$ reasoning tokens when the input size is $n$. We complement these results with matching or near-matching upper bounds via explicit constructions. Finally, our experiments with frontier reasoning models show approximately linear reasoning token scaling on these tasks and failures when constrained to smaller reasoning budgets, consistent with our theoretical lower bounds. Together, our results identify fundamental bottlenecks in inference-time compute through CoT and offer a principled tool for analyzing optimal reasoning length.
